rv.q: Yet you just cannot help but see "The Anarchist" as a cautionary tale for the writer who gains so much clout that he can now get anything up in the great American marketplace without any of the usual formative niceties, without any of the usual checks and balances.
The two actresses, seated across from each other at a plain table, engage in a battle of wills that feels more like a philosophical exercise than a fully realized drama.
When you reach the end of “Anarchist,” you may feel you’ve traveled an unnecessarily winding road to get there.
More needlessly opaque debate than drama
For all the skill with which Ms. Peet has constructed her play, it remains stubbornly static.

Some actors are more commanding than others when grappling with the exacting rhythms of David Mamet’s clipped dialogue. Patti LuPone, who collaborated with the playwright on The Old Neighborhood in 1997 and in a number of other plays and films, is a natural. Debra Winger, making her Broadway debut, is still finding her way.

Despite a career-long crusade to streamline theater by sandblasting away its airy effeminacies (like acting and emoting), his latest, The Anarchist, still feels strangely gassy, even at a Spanxed 80 minutes.
LuPone and Winger might just as well stand at lecterns, two deeply interesting, star-quality actors subsuming all that's interesting about them in service to brusque badinage between opaque symbols.
If only the same could be said of Mamet's play.

This simple setup surely could have made for a volatile, confrontational drama. But the 70-minute play is little more than a meandering and academic debate that’s hard to follow. While I won’t spoil the ending, let’s just say that it’s quick, random and heavy-handed, much like the rest of the play.
'The Anarchist' only runs 65 minutes, but I doubt there'll be any complaints that it's too short.
Mamet certainly believes in punishing his audience.

cn.t: Mamet's brief two-hander draws largely negative reviews, criticized as an inert, pedantic philosophical exercise that feels more like a debate than drama. LuPone and Winger's performances can't overcome the static, meandering script.

sg.ra: 805-seat intimate Shubert house; center Orchestra D-F is the consensus best pick across Headout, SeatPlan, and TickPick. Rows A-D play well for plays/intimate-drama given Golden's small footprint. SeatPlan notes mezzanine overhang begins at Row L with 'minimal' effect, so orchestra rear rows remain viable.
Headout and TickPick both flag center G-L as the sweet spot for value — priced below front orchestra but still before the Row L overhang line. In an 805-seat house these rows feel close regardless.

Front Mezz rows A-C center are the #2 premium pick after center orchestra — elevation gives a clean overhead line on the small Golden stage. SeatPlan flags a safety bar that can distract Row A slightly, and legroom is noted as 'slightly cramped for taller patrons.'

SeatPlan calls rear mezz 'surprisingly good' because the 805-seat footprint keeps even back rows close. Rake is described as well-designed with good elevation over Front Mezz. Legroom is the main knock — 'cramped' with narrow pitch.
